national_library_of_australia.claim: National legal deposit is a requirement of the Copyright Act 1968 (Cth); one copy of everything published in Australia goes to the National Library of Australia (NLA). Electronic publications have been covered since 2016.
national_library_of_australia.quote: One copy of everything that is published in Australia is to be given to the National Library under the legal deposit provisions of the Copyright Act 1968. In 2016 the laws were expanded to include electronic publications.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Who must deposit: any Australian person, group or organisation that distributes their work to the public, for sale or free. You do not have to be a professional publisher.
national_library_of_australia.quote: You don't have to be a publishing professional to be considered a publisher - you might for example be an individual or a community organisation. Legal deposit applies to any Australian person, group or organisation that distributes their work to the public for sale or for free.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Self-publishers are the publisher and are responsible for the deposit, even when using an overseas platform (Amazon, IngramSpark etc.).
national_library_of_australia.quote: If you are based in Australia and self-published your work using a platform or service that is based outside of Australia (e.g. Amazon, Smashwords, Ingram Spark), then your publication is required under legal deposit because you (the publisher of the work) are based in Australia.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Deposit is the publisher's responsibility, not the printer's or distributor's.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Legal deposit is always the responsibility of the publisher or self-publisher, not any other involved parties.

national_library_of_australia.claim: What must be deposited: all Australian publications made available to the public in print or electronic format, for sale or free; print books and eBooks are listed first.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Legal deposit applies to all Australian publications that have been made available to the public in a print or electronic format, whether for sale or for free. This includes: Print books and eBooks Graphic novels, comic books, and zines Newspapers, magazines, journals, and newsletters Annual reports, corporate plans, and other reports Government publications Maps Sheet music Websites

national_library_of_australia.claim: Not required: unpublished works (drafts, uncorrected proofs, advance reader copies), privately distributed works; selectively collected: blank forms, calendars and diaries, colouring/puzzle books without significant text, etc.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Uncorrected proofs and advance reader copies
national_library_of_australia.quote2: Works that have only been distributed privately
national_library_of_australia.quote3: Activity-based materials such as colouring books, puzzle books, and games that do not have significant text

national_library_of_australia.claim: Copies required by the NLA: one copy only. Duplicates are discarded.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Australian publishers are required to deposit only one copy of their publications to meet their national legal deposit obligations. Duplicate copies will be discarded in accordance with our Collection Deaccessioning and Disposal policy.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Time limit (NLA guidance): deposit within one month of publication. Late deposits are still accepted.
national_library_of_australia.quote: In accordance with the Copyright Act 1968, published works should be deposited within one month of publication. However, we understand that this is not always possible. There is no expiry date on legal deposit, so your publication will be gratefully received even if it is deposited late.

national_library_of_australia.claim: NLA fact sheet wording of the same time limit.
national_library_of_australia.quote: You should deposit your work within one month of the publication’s release date.
national_library_of_australia.note: PDF fact sheet dated Feb 2025 (file name 20250226).

national_library_of_australia.claim: Statute: the delivery period starts on the day of publication (or the day of an NLA request for online material) and ends 1 month later, or later if the Director-General allows.
national_library_of_australia.quote: (2) The delivery period, for National Library material, starts on: (a) for material published in a way covered by paragraph 195CB(1)(a) - the day it was so published; or (b) for material requested under section 195CC - the day the request was made; and ends 1 month later or on a later day allowed by the Director‑General of the National Library.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Statute outline: publishers must deliver copies to the NLA; for works available online the NLA may request delivery.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Persons publishing certain literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works in Australia must deliver copies of the works to the National Library. The National Library may also request the delivery of works that are available online.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Statutory offence for material published in Australia but NOT available online: failing to deliver within the delivery period. Strict liability, maximum 10 penalty units.
national_library_of_australia.quote: (1) A person commits an offence if: (a) the person publishes National Library material in Australia on a particular day, but not in such a way that makes the material available online; and (b) the person is not requested under section 195CC, during the period of 1 month starting on that day, to cause a copy of the material to be delivered under section 195CD; and (c) the person contravenes section 195CD. Penalty: 10 penalty units.

national_library_of_australia.claim: For material that IS available online (e.g. an ebook sold on the internet) the statutory offence only arises after the NLA requests a copy under s 195CC. NLA guidance nevertheless asks publishers to deposit ebooks through NED within a month.
national_library_of_australia.quote: (2) A person commits an offence if: (a) the person publishes National Library material; and (b) the material is available online; and (c) the person is requested under section 195CC to cause a copy of the material to be delivered under section 195CD; and (d) the person contravenes section 195CD. Penalty: 10 penalty units.
national_library_of_australia.note: The second sentence of the claim is my reading of how s 195CB(2) sits beside the NLA guidance quoted in ld.nla.time_limit; it is not legal advice.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Statutory requirements for the deposited copy: whole of the material; electronic copies free of technological protection measures (DRM); hardcopy as the best copies supplied to the public; delivered at the publisher's expense.
national_library_of_australia.quote: (c) if the copy is in an electronic form: (i) is free from any technological protection measure; and (ii) is accompanied by any software or additional information necessary for the National Library to access the material from the copy; and (d) if the copy is in hardcopy form: (i) is finished and coloured, and bound, sewed, stitched or otherwise fastened together, in the same manner as the best copies of the material are supplied to the public; and (ii) is on the best paper on which the material is printed; and (e) is delivered at the person’s own expense, unless the copy was requested under section 195CC and the request stated otherwise; and

national_library_of_australia.claim: Statute: the print and electronic forms of the same work are the same material (so one deposit covers both).
national_library_of_australia.quote: Note: The same work in hardcopy form and an electronic form is the same National Library material.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Statutory definition of what is covered includes books (in electronic form or otherwise) in which copyright subsists; new editions only if they contain additions or alterations.
national_library_of_australia.quote: A literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, or an edition of such a work, (whether in an electronic form or otherwise) is National Library material if: (a) the work or edition is: (i) a website, web page, web file, book, periodical, newspaper, pamphlet, sheet of music, map, plan, chart or table; or

national_library_of_australia.claim: The Commonwealth scheme does not displace State/Territory legal deposit laws.
national_library_of_australia.quote: This Division is not intended to exclude or limit the operation of any law of a State or Territory (whether made before or after the commencement of this Division) that makes provision for or in relation to the delivery to a specified public or other library in or of the State or Territory of copies of National Library material published in the State or Territory.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Print vs electronic: if a work is available in both, the NLA prefers the electronic version via NED, and an electronic deposit means no print copy is needed.
national_library_of_australia.quote: If your work is published and available to the public in both print and electronic formats, we prefer to collect the electronic version via National edeposit (NED). If you deposit an electronic copy of a publication via NED, you do not need to provide a print copy of the same publication.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Only one format is required nationally.
national_library_of_australia.quote: We require Australian publishers to deposit only one format of their publications to meet their legal deposit obligations. If you send multiple copies, duplicate copies may be discarded.

national_library_of_australia.claim: If only print exists and there are several print formats (hardcover, paperback), only one is required. Electronic print proofs and scans are not accepted as the electronic version.
national_library_of_australia.quote: If your work has been published in multiple print formats (e.g. hardcover, paperback, board book), we only require one format. Please provide whichever version you feel best represents the work in the way it was intended to be distributed and viewed.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Print-ready proofs/scans are not accepted in place of the published ebook.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Please note that electronic print proofs and scans will not be accepted.

national_library_of_australia.claim: New editions are deposited when they have a new edition statement, a change of publisher, a new ISBN or significant content changes; reprints, same content in a new format and minor corrections are not.
national_library_of_australia.quote: To be accepted, a new edition should have one or more of the following: An updated edition statement on the imprint page (e.g. second edition, revised edition) A change of publisher A new ISBN Significant changes to the content (e.g. new chapters) If your revised work is a reprint, the same content in a new format, or contains only minor changes or corrections, you do not need to supply a copy of the new version to the National Library of Australia.

national_library_of_australia.claim: An ISBN is not required to deposit (but is required for the Australian Lending Right schemes).
national_library_of_australia.quote: ISBNs (International Standard Book Numbers), ISSNs (International Standard Serial Numbers) or ISMNs (International Standard Music Numbers) assist in identifying your unique publication and are encouraged, but are not needed to make a deposit. ISBNs are required to be eligible for the Australian Lending Rights Scheme.

national_library_of_australia.claim: National edeposit (NED) is the NLA's preferred way to receive deposits; access conditions are set at deposit time.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Electronic deposit is quick and easy and is our preferred way to receive collection items. You can deposit an electronic copy of your publication through the National edeposit service (NED). You can set access conditions at the time of deposit.

national_library_of_australia.claim: NED portal URL: https://ned.gov.au/ned/ (the NLA page's "Go to National edeposit" button links there; https://ned.gov.au/ redirects to it; the NLA fact sheet cites it as ned.gov.au).
national_library_of_australia.quote: Go to National edeposit
national_library_of_australia.note: Link target read from the page HTML (href="https://ned.gov.au/ned/"); HTTP 200 on 2026-11-23. The NLA FAQ also links https://www.ned.gov.au/portal/ (HTTP 200).

national_library_of_australia.claim: NED is a joint service of Australia's nine national, state and territory libraries for deposit, preservation and access to published electronic material.
national_library_of_australia.quote: The NED members are the National Library of Australia, ACT Heritage Library, Libraries Tasmania, Library & Archives NT, State Library of New South Wales, State Library of Queensland, State Library of South Australia, State Library Victoria and the State Library of Western Australia.

national_library_of_australia.claim: NED deposit is free.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Electronic deposit is free, easy, safe and fast, and is our preferred way to receive collection items.

national_library_of_australia.claim: A NED deposit satisfies the national obligation; state/territory obligations may remain.
national_library_of_australia.quote: By depositing electronically, you will have met your legal deposit obligations to the National Library of Australia. You may still have obligations to your state or territory library.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Files deposited through NED must be DRM-free.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Electronic files need to be free of Digital Rights Management restrictions (DRM) so they can be preserved and made available into the future.

national_library_of_australia.claim: NED accepts .epub, .mobi and .pdf for books; .epub is preferred when several exist.
national_library_of_australia.quote: If your publication is available in more than one of these formats, our preference is .epub.
national_library_of_australia.quote2: .epub - the standard file format for ebooks in the publishing industry that enables them to be read on a wide range of devices. .mobi - an ebook file format commonly associated with Amazon Kindle devices. .pdf - one of the most used file types that preserves the look and layout of a document no matter which device or software you use to view it.

national_library_of_australia.claim: NED file size limit: under 1 GB; the portal rejects files with DRM, viruses or over 1 GB.
national_library_of_australia.quote: If the NED service detects any DRM protections, viruses or if your file is larger than 1GB, you will not be able to complete your deposit.

national_library_of_australia.claim: NED auto-generates a cover thumbnail from the file; an own cover image may be uploaded as .jpg/.jpeg or .tif/.tiff, RGB recommended.
national_library_of_australia.quote: We recommend that your cover image use the RGB colour mode, which is the primary colour mode for digital design.
national_library_of_australia.quote2: When you upload your electronic publication file the NED portal will automatically generate a cover image based on your file.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Metadata NED requires for a monograph (book).
national_library_of_australia.quote: Information that must be provided if your ePublication is a Monograph includes: Title (as shown on the title page or cover of your publication, do not use the file name as the title). Scale (if you are depositing a map). Who owns the intellectual content of the publication (author/creator). Year of publication. Edition statement (if applicable). ISBN/ISSN/ISMN (if applicable). Indicating if the publication is a work of fiction. Indicating if the publication contains sensitive information (if applicable).

national_library_of_australia.claim: The six NED deposit steps.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Choose what type of electronic publication is being deposited and upload the file. Provide information about the publication you are depositing. Nominate access conditions for the publication you are depositing. Nominate a Creative Commons licence for the publication you are depositing (optional). Provide information about you as the publisher. Review the information you have provided prior to submitting your deposit.

national_library_of_australia.claim: No account is needed for a one-off NED deposit; an account is recommended for repeat depositors.
national_library_of_australia.quote: If you wish to make a one-off deposit to NED, you do not need to create an account.

national_library_of_australia.claim: NED works in current Chrome, Firefox or Edge; Safari is not compatible.
national_library_of_australia.quote: You can use the latest two versions of Chrome, Firefox, or Edge to deposit your electronic publication. Safari is currently not compatible with the NED service.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Use the ebook's own ISBN in NED, never the print ISBN.
national_library_of_australia.quote: The ISBN for your electronic publication will be different to the ISBN for a print edition of the same publication. Do not use the print ISBN for the NED deposit.

national_library_of_australia.claim: NED offers six access conditions, from open on the internet to onsite-only at the libraries; onsite-only is available for commercially sold titles.
national_library_of_australia.quote: If your publication is available commercially, you may choose to limit access to ‘onsite only’. Choosing ‘onsite only’ means the item can be viewed, but will not be able to be downloaded, transferred, saved, printed or copied.

Openly on the Internet - with download restrictions
Openly on the Internet - with temporary download and location restrictions

national_library_of_australia.claim: NED is not a publishing platform: the ebook must already be publicly available elsewhere.
national_library_of_australia.quote: NED is not a publishing platform. If the content has not been made available to the public elsewhere it is out of scope for NED.

national_library_of_australia.claim: NED deposits usually appear in the NLA catalogue and Trove within about 48 hours, with an automatic acknowledgement.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Electronic deposits through NED are usually discoverable in our catalogue and in Trove within 48 hours.

national_library_of_australia.claim: Print deposit address for books (post, no form needed; include name and address).
national_library_of_australia.quote: Send books to: Legal Deposit National Library of Australia Parkes Place Canberra ACT 2600

national_library_of_australia.claim: Street number if a courier needs one.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Note: If a street number is required, you can include street address 25 Parkes Place W.

national_library_of_australia.claim: No form is needed for postal deposit; no acknowledgement is sent for print; print items appear in the catalogue within about 3 months.
national_library_of_australia.quote: When depositing in print by post there is no standard form to be completed, simply include your name and address on the package or on a slip with the publication.
national_library_of_australia.quote2: Your publication will appear in our catalogue and in Trove within 3 months of your date of deposit.

national_library_of_australia.claim: NLA legal deposit contact email.
national_library_of_australia.quote: Alternatively, you can email the legal deposit team at legaldeposit@nla.gov.au.

national_library_of_australia.claim: A deposit with the home state/territory library is required in addition to the NLA.
national_library_of_australia.quote: As well as depositing with us, you need to deposit your publication with your home state or territory library.

new_south_wales.claim: NSW legal deposit libraries under the Library Act 1939 (NSW): State Library of NSW, University of Sydney Library, NSW Parliamentary Library.
new_south_wales.quote: The Library Act 1939, as amended, now requires that all print and digital publications be deposited to three legal deposit libraries in NSW - the State Library of NSW, the University of Sydney Library and the NSW Parliamentary Library.

libraries: State Library of New South Wales

new_south_wales.claim: The Library Amendment Act 2019 (NSW) extended legal deposit to digital formats and repealed the Copyright Act 1879 (NSW).
new_south_wales.quote: In June 2019, the New South Wales Parliament passed the Library Amendment Act 2019. This legislation extended legal deposit to cover all published formats, including digital formats. The previous legal deposit legislation, the Copyright Act 1879 (NSW), applicable to only print formats, was repealed.

new_south_wales.claim: Who: NSW publishers, including self-publishers residing in NSW.
new_south_wales.quote: As a New South Wales or Australian Government publisher, you are required to deposit your works with the State Library. This also applies to self-publishers residing in New South Wales.

new_south_wales.claim: State Library of NSW (non-government publishers): one copy of EVERY format; if a title is published in print and digital, both must be deposited. (Stricter than the NLA, which wants one format only.)
new_south_wales.quote: The State Library requires one copy of all formats of a publication for legal deposit. If a title is published in both print and digital formats, the Library requires both versions to be deposited.

new_south_wales.claim: State Library of NSW print deposit address.
new_south_wales.quote: Send one copy to: Legal Deposit Level 2 State Library of New South Wales 1 Shakespeare Place Sydney, NSW 2000

address_lines: State Library of New South Wales

new_south_wales.claim: State Library of NSW digital deposit: one copy through NED.
new_south_wales.quote: Deposit one copy to the National edeposit (NED) service.

new_south_wales.claim: State Library of NSW legal deposit contacts.
new_south_wales.quote: contact the Library at legal.deposit@sl.nsw.gov.au or (02) 9273 1490

new_south_wales.claim: For the NSW Parliamentary Library and the University of Sydney Library, the State Library says to contact those libraries.
new_south_wales.quote: You may also be required to deposit your publications with the National Library of Australia, NSW Parliamentary Library, or the University of Sydney Library. For more information about these requirements contact the National Library of Australia, collections@parliament.nsw.gov.au or the University of Sydney Library.

new_south_wales.claim: State Library summary for non-government NSW publishers: State Library (print AND digital if both published), NSW Parliamentary Library, University of Sydney Library and the NLA; digital to the State Library and NLA goes through NED.
new_south_wales.quote: deposit their print and digital publications with the State Library of NSW (both print and digital if both published), the NSW Parliamentary Library, the University of Sydney Library and National Library of Australia. To satisfy their obligations for depositing digital publications to the State Library of NSW and the National Library of Australia, publishers should deposit to the National edeposit service - www.ned.gov.au

new_south_wales.claim: A NED deposit does not discharge the obligation to the NSW Parliamentary Library and the University of Sydney Library (neither is a NED member).
new_south_wales.quote: In New South Wales, publishers are required as well to deposit publications to the Parliamentary Library of New South Wales, the Library of the University of Sydney (except NSW Government publications) and the Western Sydney University Library (for NSW Government publications only). Depositing material through the NED deposit processes does not remove a publisher’s obligation to deposit publications with these libraries.

new_south_wales.claim: University of Sydney Library: non-government NSW publishers must OFFER a copy of all print publications; submit details and the Library advises what to send. Digital-only titles go to NED.
new_south_wales.quote: In accordance with the Library Act 1939 (NSW), all NSW non-government publishers must offer a copy of all print publications to the University of Sydney Library. This requirement includes independent and self-publishers. Publications only available in digital format are to be deposited into the National eDeposit.

new_south_wales.claim: University of Sydney process: submit publication details first.
new_south_wales.quote: If you have published a new print work in New South Wales, please submit details of your publication and we will advise you of your deposit requirements.

new_south_wales.claim: CONFLICT: the Australian Government ABLIS listing says the State Library of NSW takes two copies and that either an electronic or a physical copy may be submitted. The State Library's own page (ld.nsw.slnsw.copies) says one copy of each format, both formats if both exist. Treat the State Library page as authoritative.
new_south_wales.quote: the State Library of New South Wales (two copies)
new_south_wales.note: Conflicting official sources. "Two copies" matches the State Library's rule for NSW GOVERNMENT publications published only in print, which may be the origin of the ABLIS figure (my inference, not stated).
new_south_wales.quote2: You may either submit an electronic or physical copy.

new_south_wales.claim: NSW time limit for deposit after publication.
new_south_wales.note: NOT CONFIRMED. None of the reachable State Library of NSW, NED or University of Sydney pages states a deadline. The Library Act 1939 (NSW) could not be read: legislation.nsw.gov.au, AustLII and parliament.nsw.gov.au all answer HTTP 403 (Cloudflare challenge) to curl and to WebFetch. Search-engine summaries (unverified, not read on the official page) say the Act works through "legal deposit orders" under s 14C that "may specify a reasonable time", with a maximum penalty of 10 penalty units, i.e. possibly no fixed statutory period. Ask the State Library (legal.deposit@sl.nsw.gov.au) or read the Act before stating a NSW deadline. NED's general guidance is the only timing found: see ld.nsw.ned_timing_guidance.

new_south_wales.claim: NED general guidance on timing (all jurisdictions): deposit electronic material within 1-2 months of publication.
new_south_wales.quote: Publishers are encouraged to deposit electronic materials within 1-2 months of publication to help build the national collection.
new_south_wales.note: Guidance from the NED service, not a NSW statutory deadline.

new_south_wales.claim: NSW Parliamentary Library: number of copies, address and process.
new_south_wales.note: NOT CONFIRMED. www.parliament.nsw.gov.au answers HTTP 403 (Cloudflare challenge). Only the contact addresses given by the State Library (collections@parliament.nsw.gov.au) and ABLIS (DPS.Library@parliament.nsw.gov.au, 02 9230 2380) were found.

prepublication_data_service.claim: The NLA Prepublication Data Service (PDS), formerly Cataloguing in Publication (CiP), is a free service that puts a catalogue record for an UPCOMING Australian publication into the national database and Trove.
prepublication_data_service.quote: The Prepublication Data Service (formerly Cataloguing in Publication (CiP)) is a free service offered by the Library. This service is for Australian publishers and self-publishing authors who want the details of their upcoming publications made available to Australian libraries, library suppliers, and other members of the book industry for acquisition purposes.

prepublication_data_service.claim: Still offered as at 2026-11-23: the service page and application link are live, and the NLA legal deposit FAQ (published 20 Apr 2026) describes it in the present tense as an optional service that does not replace legal deposit.
prepublication_data_service.quote: Our Prepublication Data Service (PDS) is an optional service that you can use to have a prepublication catalogue record created for your work prior to publishing. This does not replace your legal deposit requirements; therefore, you will still need to deposit a copy of your work once it has been published.
prepublication_data_service.note: Service page HTTP 200 (page published 23 Oct 2024); application process page HTTP 200 (page published 30 May 2025); the application endpoint cipismnref.nla.gov.au answered HTTP 200 (form itself needs a browser session, not opened further).

prepublication_data_service.claim: A brief prepublication record appears in the Australian National Bibliographic Database and Trove within 48 hours of applying.
prepublication_data_service.quote: After submitting your application, a brief prepublication catalogue record is automatically generated, and will appear in Australian National Bibliographic Database and Trove, the national discovery service, within 48 hours.

prepublication_data_service.claim: Applicants receive a cataloguing statement (image) that may be printed on the imprint/copyright page. It is optional and may be resized but not otherwise altered.
prepublication_data_service.quote: The cataloguing statement should be printed on the imprint page with the publication details and copyright information. This is usually located on the reverse side of the title page.

prepublication_data_service.claim: Rules for the cataloguing statement artwork.
prepublication_data_service.quote: The cataloguing statement may be resized (with constraints maintained), ranged left or centred to suit your design arrangements. The cataloguing statement may not be altered in any other way.

prepublication_data_service.claim: Eligible: upcoming books published in Australia, including ebooks, self-published and print-on-demand books. Not eligible: books already published, books published overseas, unchanged reprints.
prepublication_data_service.quote: To be eligible for the Prepublication Data Service, your upcoming publication should be published in Australia. If you are Australian and you have self-published, you are considered to be the publisher even if your book was printed overseas.
prepublication_data_service.quote3: Reprints where the imprint, publisher, content and format are unchanged

prepublication_data_service.quote: Books that have already been published

prepublication_data_service.claim: The PDS form uses a defined selection of Thema subjects: one fiction subject or up to two non-fiction subjects.
prepublication_data_service.quote: You may select one fiction subject or up to two non-fiction subjects.
prepublication_data_service.quote2: The Prepublication Data Service form uses a defined selection of Thema subjects.

prepublication_data_service.claim: The NLA does not change prepublication records after submission, so the data must be right first time.
prepublication_data_service.quote: Please ensure your application has the most accurate and up-to-date information possible as we do not make changes to prepublication catalogue records.

prepublication_data_service.claim: The PDS reference number (NLAppxxxx) pre-fills the NED deposit form.
prepublication_data_service.quote: Take note of your reference number (NLAppxxxx) contained in your confirmation email after submitting your online PDS application, as this is needed if you also deposit via NED.

prepublication_data_service.claim: PDS enquiries are by online form only; response within 10 working days.
prepublication_data_service.quote: We can no longer be contacted directly by telephone. You will receive a response within 10 working days.

text: Ebook edition: deposit one DRM-free EPUB (preferred) through NED (https://ned.gov.au/ned/) using the ebook ISBN. That meets the NLA obligation and the State Library of NSW digital obligation.

Print edition: the NLA does not need it if the ebook went to NED; the State Library of NSW still wants one print copy (Legal Deposit, Level 2, State Library of New South Wales, 1 Shakespeare Place, Sydney NSW 2000).
University of Sydney Library: offer the print edition via its form; it replies with what to send.
NSW Parliamentary Library: contact collections@parliament.nsw.gov.au (requirements not confirmed).
Print-only title: one print copy to the NLA (Legal Deposit, National Library of Australia, Parkes Place, Canberra ACT 2600) within one month of publication, plus the NSW libraries.
NLA deadline is one month from publication; no NSW deadline could be confirmed.

facts.claim: International rule: the publisher must give its ISBN agency at least these metadata elements for each ISBN. Mandatory: ISBN, product form, title, language(s) of text, imprint, publisher, country of publication, publication date (and edition number after the first edition). Optional: series, contributor(s), product form detail/features, measurements, parent ISBN.
facts.quote: It is the responsibility of publishers/registrants to inform their ISBN registration agency, or organisation responsible for the maintenance of publication registration, of the ISBNs that will be assigned to forthcoming publications. The information shall include the following minimum metadata (descriptive) elements and shall be compatible with the ONIX for Books product information standards maintained by EDItEUR and its associated organisations:
facts.note: The manual prints this as a table; the value block transcribes its rows (table cells are separate lines in the saved text). What Thorpe-Bowker's form actually asks for is not confirmed.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual, 7th edition (2017), section 8

mandatory.comment: In the 13-digit ISBN format, without spaces or hyphens
Coding which indicates the medium and/or format of the product
The title of the publication, together with sub-title or other title elements where applicable
Edition number (for editions after the first), type, and statement
The brand name under which the publication is published
The person or organisation that owns the imprint at the date of publication
The date of first publication under this ISBN. In the ISO 8601 format (YYYYMMDD).

facts.claim: The national agency tells the publisher which metadata is required and how to submit it.
facts.quote: Publishers must supply the national ISBN agency (or its designated local bibliographic agency) with a specified amount of metadata about the publication (such as title, author, format etc) to which the ISBN is assigned.

facts.claim: Each separate edition or format needs its own ISBN.
facts.quote: A separate ISBN shall be assigned to each separate monographic publication or separate edition or format of a monographic publication issued by a publisher.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 6.1

facts.claim: Hardback vs paperback, and PDF vs EPUB, are changes that require a separate ISBN.
facts.quote: product form (e.g., from hardback to paperback; from audiobook on a physical carrier to audiobook available to download) product form detail (e.g., from .pdf to EPUB; change of book dimension)
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 6.2

facts.claim: Each ebook file format that is separately available (EPUB, PDF) should have its own ISBN.
facts.quote: Where a specific qualifying e-book is available in different underlying file formats such as EPUB, .pdf etc., each different format that is published and made separately available should be given a separate ISBN.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 9.3

facts.claim: A retailer-exclusive proprietary format (e.g. Amazon Kindle) does not strictly need an ISBN; if one is assigned it must be unique to that version.
facts.quote: However, where digital publications are being supplied by a retailer that is the sole provider of e-books in a proprietary format that can only be bought through their own websites (e.g. Amazon Kindle, Apple i-books) and that retailer does not require ISBNs, it may not be necessary to assign ISBNs to those versions.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 9.3

facts.claim: The same EPUB sold through several retailers with substantially the same usage constraints uses a single ISBN.
facts.quote: If the different versions are in the same format and use the same DRM software (e.g. Adobe ACS4) with substantially the same usage constraints and are interoperable on different devices or software, then a single ISBN should be used.

facts.claim: How to list the ISBNs of all formats on the copyright page.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 13.1

facts.claim: No new ISBN for a price change, a cover change or an unchanged reprint.
facts.quote: A change to the cover design or colour or to the price of a monographic publication does not require a separate ISBN, although a separate ISBN may be assigned if required by the supply chain (e.g., media tie-in).
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 6.2
facts.quote2: A separate ISBN should not be assigned to an unchanged edition or unchanged reprint of the same publication, issued in the same product form, product form detail, product form feature, with the same usage constraints, by the same publisher or imprint.

facts.claim: A new ISBN is needed for a change of title/subtitle, language, publisher or imprint, author name, or textual content beyond minor corrections.
facts.quote: the title and/or the subtitle of a publication language publisher name or imprint author name textual content other than minor corrections to misprints
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 6.2

facts.claim: Print on demand is just a print technology: same ISBN unless the product form changes; minor trim-size changes for POD machines need no new ISBN.
facts.quote: Minor changes to trim sizes in order to comply with the specifications of on-demand printing machines do not require a new ISBN.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 10

facts.claim: If a platform supplies the ISBN, the platform is likely to be listed as the publisher; own ISBNs come from the agency of the country where the publisher is based.
facts.quote: Self-publishers should be aware that if a third-party service provider offers to assign one of their range of ISBNs, then that service provider is likely to be listed as the publisher in ISBN-related databases.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 12
facts.quote2: N.B. ISBNs should be obtained from the appropriate ISBN registration agency responsible for the country in which the publisher is based, regardless of the location of any platform or self-publishing service.

facts.claim: An ISBN can never be reused or transferred to another publisher.
facts.quote: Once assigned to a monographic publication, an ISBN can never be reused to identify another monographic publication, even if the original ISBN is found to have been assigned in error.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 7.8

facts.claim: Where the ISBN must appear on a printed book, and minimum type size.
facts.quote: In the case of printed publications, the ISBN must appear on the: Verso of the title page (copyright page) Foot of the title page, if there is no space on the title verso Lower section of the outside back cover Foot of the back of the jacket, or any other protective case, or wrapper
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 13.1
facts.quote2: The ISBN should always be printed in type large enough to be easily legible (i.e., 9-point or larger).

facts.claim: When printed, the ISBN is preceded by "ISBN" and its five elements are separated by hyphens or spaces.
facts.quote: When printed, the ISBN is always preceded by the letters “ISBN”.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 5
facts.quote2: The elements should each be separated clearly by hyphens or spaces when displayed in human readable form:

facts.claim: The ISBN is encoded as an EAN-13 barcode; the human-readable ISBN, preceded by "ISBN", goes immediately above the symbol.
facts.quote: When used in a bar code, the ISBN must be displayed in human readable form immediately above the EAN-13 bar code symbol, preceded by “ISBN”.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 13.2

facts.claim: Recommended barcode position: lower right quadrant of the back cover, near the spine.
facts.quote: The recommended location of the EAN-13 bar code symbol for publications is the lower right quadrant of the back, near the spine.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 13.2

facts.claim: No GS1 membership is needed to print an ISBN as a barcode.
facts.quote: If you only want to use the ISBN in bar-coded form, you do not have to become a member of GS1 in order to do so.

facts.claim: GS1 Australia: an ISBN is already a GTIN, so no separate GS1 number is needed for a book.
facts.quote: As the ISBN is incorporated in the GTIN standard, you do not need to assign a separate GTIN in addition to the ISBN to your product.

facts.claim: KEY RULE FOR AUSTRALIA: the International ISBN Agency says the five-digit add-on is used for price only in the United States and Canada and should NOT be used for price information in other countries; elsewhere it may only carry a publisher's in-house code in the range 90000-98999.
facts.quote: In the United States and Canada, a five-digit add-on to the bar code is used in the book trade to indicate the price. For further information on bar codes in the United States and Canada visit the Book Industry Study Group website http://bisg.org. The five-digit add-on code should not be used for price information in other countries, although it may be used with a “9” prefix for a publisher’s own in-house use (e.g., for handling returns). These supplementary codes always start with “9” within the range “90000-98999”.
facts.section: ISBN Users' Manual 7th ed., section 13.3

facts.claim: Nominal (100%) X-dimension of EAN-13: 0.330 mm.
facts.quote: The X-dimension at nominal size is 0.330 millimetre (0.0130 inch).
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.2.3.1

facts.claim: Nominal EAN-13 size: 37.29 mm wide (113 modules including both quiet zones) with 22.85 mm bar height.
facts.quote: an EAN-13 symbol with an X-dimension of 0.330 mm (0.0130 inch), its nominal dimension, has a width of 37.29 mm (1.468 inch) and a bar height of 22.85 mm (0.900 inch).
facts.note: 37.29 mm = 113 modules x 0.330 mm, i.e. it includes the 11X and 7X quiet zones (GS1 Table 5-12 gives EAN-13 length 113 modules "including the minimum Quiet Zones"). The bars alone are 31.35 mm wide (GS1 Australia fact sheet, bc.nominal.gs1au).
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.12.2.2

facts.claim: GS1 Australia table row for 100%: X 0.33 mm, width 31.35 mm excluding quiet zones, bar height 22.85 mm, left quiet zone 3.63 mm, right quiet zone 2.31 mm.
facts.section: GS1 Australia EAN-13 barcode Fact Sheet, August 2026, Table 1
facts.quote2: Width = width of barcode excluding Quiet Zones.

facts.claim: Bar height at nominal size is 22.85 mm; guard bars extend a further 5X (1.65 mm) downward. The human-readable digits are not part of the specified height.
facts.quote: For EAN-13, UPC-A and UPC-E barcodes the height of the symbol at the nominal size is 22.85 millimetres (0.900 inch).
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.2.3.2

facts.claim: Overall nominal height including human-readable digits (often quoted as 25.93 mm).
facts.note: NOT CONFIRMED in text. The GS1 General Specifications give the overall figure only in a dimensioned drawing (section 5.2.6.6), which is an image and did not survive text extraction. Use the text-verified figures: 37.29 mm x 22.85 mm bar height plus 5X guard-bar extension.

facts.claim: Allowed size range at retail point of sale: 80% to 200% of nominal (X-dimension 0.264 mm to 0.660 mm; target 0.330 mm).
facts.quote: Retail POS: 80% - 200% (X-dimension 0.26mm - 0.66mm).
facts.section: GS1 Australia EAN-13 barcode Fact Sheet, August 2026

facts.claim: GS1 global symbol specification table 1 row for EAN-13 and EAN-13 + 5: X min 0.264 / target 0.330 / max 0.660 mm; minimum bar height 18.28 / 22.85 / 45.70 mm; quiet zones 11X left, 7X right.
facts.note: In the +5 row the columns are: left quiet zone 11X, minimum separation between symbols 7X, maximum separation 12X, right quiet zone 5X.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.12.3.1 Table 5-44

facts.claim: GS1 no longer specifies "magnification"; it specifies X-dimension. 100% = 0.330 mm.
facts.quote: The term magnification has been used to refer to a range of sizes below, at, or above the nominal dimension (100% magnification) for EAN/UPC symbols used in the omnidirectional scanning environment. The symbol specification tables (SSTs) do not use magnification values and instead list the target, minimum and maximum values for the symbol's X-dimension and height.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.12.2.2

facts.claim: Below 80% (X 0.249-0.264 mm) is allowed only for on-demand (thermal, laser) printing.
facts.quote: The allowance for X-dimensions between 0.249 millimetre (0.0098 inch) and 0.264 millimetre (0.0104 inch) is only applicable to on demand (e.g., thermal, laser) print processes.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, Table 5-44 note (*)

facts.claim: Bar height may be truncated for packaging reasons but not below 60% of the minimum height for the X-dimension (GS1 Australia).
facts.quote: the symbol height SHALL NOT be reduced below 60% of the minimum height specified for the applicable X-dimension.

facts.claim: Quiet zones for EAN-13: left 11 modules (3.63 mm at nominal), right 7 modules (2.31 mm). After an add-on: 5 modules (1.65 mm). Gap between main symbol and add-on: 7 to 12 modules.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.2.3.4 Table 5-11

facts.claim: General minimum quiet zone for the main symbol.
facts.quote: The minimum Quiet Zone width required by the main symbol is 7x.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.2.3.4

facts.claim: Symbol lengths in modules including minimum quiet zones: EAN-13 = 113; five-digit add-on = 52; EAN-13 + five-digit add-on = 165 (54.45 mm at nominal).
facts.quote: EAN-13 or UPC-A and five-digit add-on 165
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.2.3.5 Table 5-12

facts.claim: EAN-13 structure: left quiet zone, normal guard, six characters from sets A/B, centre guard, six characters from set C, normal guard, right quiet zone; the 13th (leading) digit is encoded by the A/B parity pattern.
facts.quote: The EAN-13 barcode SHALL be made up as follows, reading from left to right: ■ A left Quiet Zone. ■ A normal guard bar pattern. ■ Six symbol characters from number sets A and B. ■ A centre guard bar pattern. ■ Six symbol characters from number set C. ■ A normal guard bar pattern. ■ A right Quiet Zone.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.2.2.1

facts.claim: Structure of the five-digit add-on (EAN-5): add-on guard pattern, then five digits from number sets A or B separated by add-on delineators, then a right quiet zone. No right guard bars and no explicit check digit.
facts.quote: A five-digit add-on symbol may be used in specific applications to accompany an EAN-13, UPC-A, or UPC-E barcode. The five-digit add-on symbol is positioned following the right Quiet Zone of the main symbol and consists of the following: 1. Add-on guard bar pattern. 2. First digit of the add-on number from number sets A or B. 3. Add-on delineator. 4. Second digit of the add-on number from number sets A or B. 5. Add-on delineator. 6. Third digit of the add-on number from number sets A or B. 7. Add-on delineator. 8. Fourth digit of the add-on number from number sets A or B. 9. Add-on delineator. 10. Fifth digit of the add-on number from number sets A or B. 11. A right Quiet Zone.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.2.2.5.2
facts.quote2: Add-on guard bar pattern 4 1 1 2 Add-on delineator 2 1 1

facts.claim: EAN-5 parity check: V = units digit of 3 x (d1 + d3 + d5) + 9 x (d2 + d4); V selects the A/B pattern of the five digits.
facts.quote: The add-on symbol has no right guard bar pattern. It does not have an explicit check digit. Checking is done through the mix of the number sets (A or B) used for the five digits. A value V is determined by the following procedure: 1. Sum the digits in Positions one, three and five. 2. Multiply the result of step 1 by 3. 3. Sum the remaining digits (Positions two and four). 4. Multiply the result of step 3 by 9. 5. Sum the results of steps 2 and 4.
facts.note: parity_table_V_to_sets transcribes GS1 Table 5-9 (cells are whitespace-separated in the saved text). Step 6 of the procedure ("The value of V is the unit's position (lowest-order digit) of the result of step.") follows a page break in the PDF.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.2.2.5.2 and Table 5-9
facts.quote2: Since V = 3 in Table 5-9, the sequence of number sets used to encode the value 86104 is B A A A B.

facts.claim: Add-on placement: must not encroach on the main symbol's right quiet zone; at most 12X away; bottom of its bars aligned with the bottom of the main symbol's guard bars; same X-dimension; not taller than the main symbol.
facts.quote: The add-on symbol SHALL NOT encroach on the right Quiet Zone of the main symbol. The maximum separation SHALL be 12X. The bottom edge of the bars (dark bars) in the add-on symbol SHALL be horizontally aligned with the bottom edge of the guard bars of the main symbol.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 5.2.3.6
facts.quote2: The X-dimension of an add-on symbol SHALL be the same as the X- dimension of its associated main symbol.

facts.claim: GS1 assigns NO meaning to the add-on digits: content is defined by the publisher, reading it at point of sale is optional, and it must not carry information that belongs in the GTIN.
facts.quote: The supplementary information consists of numeric data of any structure and meaning. It is the publisher's responsibility to define the numbering scheme. The data carrier for this element string is the five-digit add-on symbol.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 2.1.3.4
facts.quote2: The reading of the add-on symbol by the retailer's point-of-sale system is optional.

facts.claim: GS1: books should carry EAN-13 (or UPC); the 2- or 5-digit add-on is optional. ISBNs use GS1 prefix 978 or 979.
facts.quote: Individual books and paperbacks SHOULD be marked with an EAN-13, UPC-A, or UPC-E barcode that complies with the print quality specifications applicable to all GS1 system barcodes. The EAN/UPC 2-digit or 5-digit Add-on symbols are options used with the above EAN/UPC symbols.
facts.section: GS1 General Specifications Standard, Release 26.0, Ratified, Jan 2026, 2.1.3.4
facts.quote2: ISBN using GS1 Prefix 978 or 979

facts.claim: Currency indicator as originally designed (1980s), per BISG: leading 0 and 1 = UK pounds sterling; 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 = currencies of other English-speaking countries; 5 = US dollars; 6 = Canadian dollars; 9 = internal and industry-wide uses.
facts.quote: When the Bookland EAN was configured in the 1980s, the leading digit of the 5-digit Add-On bar code was designated as the currency indicator. Leading digits of ‘0’ and ‘1’ were assigned to UK pounds sterling, while leading digits of ‘2’, ‘3’, ‘4’, ‘5’, and ‘6’ were assigned to the currencies of other English speaking countries. A leading digit of ‘5’ was assigned to US dollars, and a leading digit of ‘6’ to Canadian dollars. A leading digit of ‘9’ was set aside for internal use by organizations in the supply chain and for some industry-wide uses.
facts.section: BISG Machine Readable Coding Committee, "Dollar Price Limit Increase in the Bookland EAN Add-On Bar Code", (c) 2005
